transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-03-12 16:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Lydia Chang (Redwood AE), Marcus Velez (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Head of ML - Pioneer Edge), Jenna Morris (Platform Eng), Koji Tanaka (CTO)

Optional auto sections present: Summary, Topics, Action items, Questions

00:00 Lydia Chang: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lydia, AE on the account, and Marcus is our SE. Appreciate you taking the time, Samir, Jenna, Koji. How's the afternoon?
00:07 Samir Patel: Hey Lydia, good thanks. Excited to see how you handle open models — we've been evaluating a few things and want to understand fit to our latency and cost targets.
00:15 Lydia Chang: Great, quick agenda: console walk, model gateway and compatibility grid, bench approach, and then Optimize suggestions — batching, quantization — and we finish with next steps. Sound okay?
00:25 Koji Tanaka: Yes, please, and I'd like a quick note on network/VPC and compliance early on.
00:30 Lydia Chang: Totally — we'll touch on that when we cover Private options. Marcus, quick intro?
00:34 Marcus Velez: Hi all, Marcus here. I'll dig into the runtime, kernel mapping, and how we interpret the compatibility matrix when picking model variants for your load. Expect a few perf graphs.
00:44 Jenna Morris: Perfect. We're particularly sensitive to p95 latency — user-facing inference — and also data residency.

01:05 Lydia Chang: Okay, starting Console. (screen share) At the top is our model gateway — think of it as the selection layer: you can filter by architecture, sequence length, and 'compatibility score' which maps to our recorded kernel/driver fit for each GPU family. This is not just model size; it's runtime fit.
01:25 Samir Patel: When you say compatibility score, is that based on your internal bench runs or vendor metrics?
01:29 Marcus Velez: It's primarily empirical. We run microbenchmarks across our fleet — different GPU SKUs, quantization modes — and we compute a profile. There are heuristics for KV cache behavior too. Sometimes the transcriptions of docs say K V cache, so apologies if you see odd labels in exports.
01:43 Samir Patel: (laughs) noted. How do you handle sequence length variability? Our prompts vary a lot.
01:48 Marcus Velez: Good question. The matrix includes a 'sequence shape' distribution — short, medium, long — and we show recommended model + quantization. For example, if 90% of your calls are sub-128 tokens, a quantized 16-bit or 8-bit profile may be best for cost.

02:12 Lydia Chang: Switching to a concrete example: here's an open instruction-tuned model in the catalog. Console shows bench numbers: p50 65ms, p95 210ms on a G5X-like SKU, tokens/sec 130, cost estimate... it's rough order of magnitude. We always recommend running a customer bench to get exact numbers.
02:32 Jenna Morris: That G5X SKU — does Redwood host or can we run on our Dedicated pool?
02:36 Marcus Velez: Both. Hosted gives you fastest time-to-value. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and consistent p95, which helps with SLOs. Private deployment can pin to your VPC for compliance. There are tradeoffs: Dedicated is usually lower jitter; Hosted may be slightly cheaper because of dynamic bin packing.
02:52 Koji Tanaka: For our use case, predictable p95 is higher priority than marginal cost — leaning toward Dedicated, but want to see numbers first.
03:00 Lydia Chang: Totally fair. We'll scope a Dedicated pilot in the next steps.

03:20 Marcus Velez: Now I'll pull up the compatibility matrix. (screen share) Columns are model family, quantization profile, observed kernels, and a compatibility rating per hardware family. Note — some models hit best performance on one GPU kernel path, others prefer an alternative kernel when KV cache is heavy.
03:39 Samir Patel: Can you show an example where a smaller model ends up being better cost/perf than a larger model?
03:44 Marcus Velez: Sure — here: Model A (7B quant 8-bit) has lower p50 but much higher tokens/sec than Model B (13B q4). For short-call workloads Model A wins on cost per inference; for long-context summarization Model B is better due to improved quality per token. It's in the console as a 'cost-adjusted quality' metric.
04:06 Lydia Chang: That's where Redwood Optimize comes in — we surface recommendations: batching window suggestions, suggested quantization (q4, q8), and kernel affinity settings. You can A/B compare models in the Console and see a simulated monthly spend.

04:28 Jenna Morris: On A/B: can we route a percentage of traffic to different model variants? Also, how does fallback work if the chosen model is unavailable?
04:35 Marcus Velez: Yes, you can do canary and percentage rollouts. Fallback is policy driven — e.g., fall back to a compatible model variant in another region or a lower-capacity tier. The Runtime will automatically swap in a model with compatible output shape when possible.

05:00 Samir Patel: About benching: what inputs do you need from us to run a representative test?
05:05 Marcus Velez: Ideally a sample of 200–500 prompts reflecting distribution (short/medium/long), expected concurrency, and SLOs. We'll run p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), and cost per 1k tokens. We'll also run quantized variants.
05:20 Samir Patel: Okay we'll export that. Also, our compliance team wants KMS integration and audit logs.
05:25 Lydia Chang: We support KMS/HSM integrations on Private and Dedicated; audit logs are available in the Console with retention options. We'll share the SOC2 package and a network diagram.

05:45 Koji Tanaka: Any obvious integration pain points? For example, peering VPCs with our cloud account?
05:50 Marcus Velez: Some customers need a peering tunnel and specific egress allowances. On Private we give a control plane shim that runs in your VPC and the inference plane inside your network. We do have on-prem installers for air-gapped environments but that's a larger project.

06:15 Lydia Chang: Back to Optimize: here's a concrete recommendation for your sample workload — batch window 25ms, q4_0 for short tokens, and enable prefix caching for stable prompts to reduce repeat costs. This cuts unit cost by ~28% in our sim.
06:31 Jenna Morris: How safe is function/tool calling and structured output with quantized models? We need deterministic outputs for some downstream parsing.
06:39 Marcus Velez: Parsing is mostly model dependent. Quantization can slightly change generation, so for deterministic output we recommend: keep critical parse tasks on higher-precision variant, or use reranking/validator pass. Console lets you pin a parse model route and a cheaper generator route for bulk tasks.
06:58 Samir Patel: Sounds good. And latency SLOs — any historical data on p95 jitter for Hosted vs Dedicated?
07:05 Marcus Velez: Typical hosted p95 jitter is 25–40ms depending on region; Dedicated p95 jitter is often <15ms because of reserved instances and reduced noisy neighbors. We'll include sample histograms in the bench report.

07:28 Lydia Chang: Quick detour — competitors. You mentioned Anthropic and OpenAI earlier. We position Redwood as production-first with model routing and cost control, and a unified console across hosted/dedicated/private.
07:44 Koji Tanaka: Understood. We will still evaluate Vertices and others, but your routing and cost tooling are interesting.

08:00 Marcus Velez: I'll show a short live bench run — low fidelity demo to illustrate the bench UI. (runs console simulated bench) You can see p50/p95, tokens/sec, and then a cost estimate pane. Note there can be transcription errors in auto-exports sometimes — that's more Fireflies than us — so take the CSV as raw and we can provide cleaned outputs.
08:26 Samir Patel: I noticed the report includes kernel mapping — what happens if a kernel isn't present on a customer's Dedicated GPU?
08:32 Marcus Velez: We map to the nearest compatible kernel path. If it's unavailable we'll recommend either a different quantization profile or a different model that hits the available kernel efficiently. There are occasional edge cases with newer ops where we need to compile a specialized path — we can do that as part of onboarding.

08:58 Jenna Morris: For pilot scope, what does Redwood need to guarantee cost visibility?
09:02 Lydia Chang: We'll enable token-level cost breakdowns for the test period. That gives you per-route cost, per-model cost, and per-token accounting.
09:09 Koji Tanaka: Good. On security docs — can you send SOC2, encryption-at-rest details, and the trust boundary diagram?
09:15 Lydia Chang: Absolutely. We'll attach those to the follow-up.

09:28 Marcus Velez: Wrapping up bench methodology: we'll run three variants — hosted baseline, dedicated baseline, and a quantized variant — using your sample prompts under target concurrency. Expect a 48–72 hour turnaround for initial runs, depending on availability.
09:45 Samir Patel: That's fine. We're aiming to decide by end of month.
09:49 Lydia Chang: Great. Quick recap and next steps: 1) Samir to send prompt set and SLOs; 2) Lydia to send pricing and SOC2/KMS docs; 3) Marcus to run bench and share results; 4) Jenna to confirm networking constraints. We'll set a 90-minute bench review the week after results.
10:10 Koji Tanaka: Works for me. Any blockers on your side?
10:13 Lydia Chang: Not stage-wise. We'll just need those artifacts from you.

10:25 (brief crosstalk about calendar invites)
10:35 Lydia Chang: Okay one last question — any concerns about model quality vs cost we didn't address?
10:40 Samir Patel: Only that for some generation tasks we might prefer an ensemble approach — generate on cheaper models and validate on a more expensive one. But that may add latency.
10:48 Marcus Velez: Exactly. You can compose routes: cheap generator + validator combo, with a fallback to high-precision parse model when validator confidence is low. Console and the routing policy handle that.

11:05 Lydia Chang: Alright thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and bench invite.
11:10 Samir Patel: Thanks, this was helpful.
11:12 Jenna Morris: Thanks all.
11:13 Koji Tanaka: Thanks.

Meeting ended.

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional transcribe errors on technical terms (e.g., 'K V cache' vs 'KV cache'), speaker overlap, and some numeric values in the bench demo were synthetic for demo only.

End of transcript.
